{{short description|Origami folding pattern}}
[[File:Miura-Ori CP.svg|thumb|[[Crease pattern]] for a Miura fold. The parallelograms of this example have 84° and 96° angles.]]
[[File:Miura-ori.gif|thumb|Animation of the folding and unfolding of a Miura-creased material]]

The {{nihongo|'''Miura fold'''|ミウラ折り|Miura-ori}} is a method of folding a flat surface such as a sheet of paper into a smaller area. The fold is named for its inventor, Japanese astrophysicist [[Kōryō Miura]].<ref>{{citation|first=Peter|last=Forbes|title=The Gecko's Foot: How Scientists are Taking a Leaf from Nature's Book|publisher=Harper Perennial|year=2006|pages=181–195}}.</ref>

The [[crease pattern]]s of the Miura fold form a [[tessellation]] of the surface by [[parallelogram]]s. In one direction, the creases lie along straight lines, with each parallelogram forming the [[Reflection symmetry|mirror reflection]] of its neighbor across each crease. In the other direction, the creases zigzag, and each parallelogram is the [[Translation (geometry)|translation]] of its neighbor across the crease. Each of the zigzag paths of creases consists solely of [[mountain fold]]s or of [[valley fold]]s, with mountains alternating with valleys from one zigzag path to the next. Each of the straight paths of creases alternates between mountain and valley folds.<ref name="bain80">{{citation |last=Bain |first=Ian |title=The Miura-Ori map |journal=[[New Scientist]] |year=1980 |url=https://www.britishorigami.org/cp-resource/the-miura-ori-map/}}. Reproduced in ''British Origami'', 1981, and online at the British Origami Society web site.</ref> 
The Miura fold is related to the [[Kresling fold]], the [[Yoshimura fold]] and the Hexagonal fold, and can be framed as a generalization of these folds.<ref>{{citation|last=Reid|first=Austin|date=2017|title=Geometry and design of origami bellows with tunable response|journal=Physical Review E|volume=95|issue=1|article-number=013002|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.95.013002|pmid=28208390|arxiv=1609.01354|bibcode=2017PhRvE..95a3002R|s2cid=20057718}}</ref> 

The Miura fold is a form of [[rigid origami]], meaning that the fold can be carried out by a continuous motion in which, at each step, each parallelogram is completely flat. This property allows it to be used to fold surfaces made of rigid materials, making it distinct from the [[Kresling fold]] and [[Yoshimura fold]] which cannot be rigidly folded and require panel [[Deformation (science)|deformations]] to compress to a compact state.<ref>{{citation|last=Kidambi|first=Narayanan|date=2020|title=Dynamics of Kresling Origami Deployment|journal=Physical Review E|volume=101|issue=6|article-number=063003|doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.101.063003|pmid=32688523|arxiv=2003.10411|bibcode=2020PhRvE.101f3003K|s2cid=214611719}}</ref> For instance, large [[solar panel]] arrays for space satellites in the [[Japanese space program]] have been Miura folded before launch and then spread out in space.<ref name=miura85>{{citation
 | last = Miura | first = K.
 | publisher = The Institute of Space and Astronautical Science
 | series = Tech. Report 618
 | title = Method of packaging and deployment of large membranes in space
 | year = 1985}}</ref>  A folded Miura fold can be packed into a compact shape, its thickness reflecting only the thickness of the folded material. Folded material can be unpacked in one motion by pulling on its opposite ends, and likewise folded by pushing the two ends together. In the solar array application, this property reduces the number of [[Electric motor|motor]]s required to unfold this shape, reducing weight and complexity.

== Applications ==
The 1996 [[Space Flyer Unit]] deployed the 2D Array from a Miura folded configuration.<ref name=jaxa>{{citation |publisher=Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051125174630/http://www.isas.jaxa.jp/e/enterp/missions/complate/sfu/2dsa.shtml |url=http://www.isas.jaxa.jp/e/enterp/missions/complate/sfu/2dsa.shtml |archive-date=25 November 2005|title=2D Array}}</ref>

The inflatable membrane structure of the SPROUT satellite is carried into space in the Miura-folded state, and then deployed using inflatable tubes themselves carried into space in the Octagon-folded state.<ref name=nihon>{{citation |url=http://sat.aero.cst.nihon-u.ac.jp/sprout-e/1-Mission-e.html |title=SPROUT Nano Satellite Project |access-date=2016-08-01 |archive-date=2017-10-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171021081726/http://sat.aero.cst.nihon-u.ac.jp/sprout-e/1-Mission-e.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=eoport>{{citation |url=https://directory.eoportal.org/web/eoportal/satellite-missions/s/sprout |title=SPROUT (Space Research on Unique Technology) |archive-date=1 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160501182514/https://directory.eoportal.org/web/eoportal/satellite-missions/s/sprout}}</ref>

Other potential applications of this fold include surgical devices such as [[stent]]s and flat-foldable furniture.<ref name=scidaily>{{citation |url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/01/160126175042.htm |title=Designing a pop-up future: Simple origami fold may hold the key to designing pop-up furniture, medical devices and scientific tools |work=Science News |publisher=[[Science Daily]] |date=January 26, 2016}}</ref>

Researchers at the [[University of Fribourg]] used the Miura fold to stack [[hydrogel]] films, generating electricity similarly to [[electric eel]]s. The Miura fold is used to cause many parts of the stack to contact each other simultaneously.<ref name=mayer17>{{citation|last1=Mayer|first1=Michael|last2=Yang|first2=Jerry|last3=Shtein|first3=Max|last4=Sept|first4=David|last5=VanRenterghem|first5=Gloria|last6=Lamoureux|first6=Aaron|last7=Guha|first7=Anirvan|last8=Schroeder|first8=Thomas B. H.|date=December 2017|title=An electric-eel-inspired soft power source from stacked hydrogels|url= |journal=Nature|language=en|volume=552|issue=7684|pages=214–218|doi=10.1038/nature24670|pmid=29239354|issn=1476-4687|pmc=6436395|bibcode=2017Natur.552..214S}}</ref>
